title: Hardness and Complexity Transition of Noisy Random Circuit Sampling
authors: Byeongseon Go, Changhun Oh, Hyunseok Jeong
abstract: Random circuit sampling (RCS) is a leading candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage, supported by strong complexity-theoretic evidence of hardness in the ideal setting and by rapid experimental progress to date. In practice, however, noise is unavoidable, and a central problem is to identify the noise-strength boundary between classically simulable and classically hard regimes. In this work, we establish an architecture-general hardness bound for this boundary for the standard local depolarizing noise of strength $γ$. Assuming the standard average-case #P-hardness conjecture for ideal RCS, we show that, for any circuit architecture satisfying this conjecture, noisy RCS on the same architecture remains hard to simulate classically within any inverse-polynomial total variation distance whenever $γ=O(\log n/(nd))$ for $n$-qubit circuits of depth $d$, unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. Crucially, noisy-RCS hardness follows without any additional conjectural or architecture-specific assumption beyond those already entering the ideal-RCS hardness framework. Our proof combines a low-degree polynomial extrapolation with a monotonicity reduction showing that efficient classical simulation at one depolarizing noise strength implies efficient simulation at every larger strength. Together, these ingredients transfer the standard ideal-RCS hardness conjecture to sampling hardness at a prespecified noise strength. Finally, combining the convergence-to-uniformity result of Dalzell et al. [Commun. Math. Phys. 405, 78 (2024)] with our monotonicity reduction yields efficient classical simulation for $γ=ω(\log n/(nd))$ on layered, regularly connected architectures. Thus, wherever the two architectural settings overlap, this identifies $γ=Θ(\log n/(nd))$ as the asymptotic complexity-transition scale.
summary: This paper rigorously establishes a complexity-theoretic threshold for Random Circuit Sampling under realistic depolarizing noise. By combining polynomial extrapolation with a monotonicity argument, the authors show that RCS remains classically hard to simulate up to a specific noise strength $\gamma = \Theta(\log n/(nd))$. This identifies this scale as the asymptotic boundary between quantum advantage and classical simulation feasibility.
main_problem: The central problem is determining the noise-strength boundary that separates regimes where Random Circuit Sampling (RCS) remains classically hard to simulate from those where it becomes efficiently simulable.
main_result: The authors establish that noisy RCS remains classically hard to simulate within an inverse-polynomial total variation distance for noise strengths $\gamma = O(\log n/(nd))$, unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses.
method: The proof combines a low-degree polynomial extrapolation technique with a monotonicity reduction, transferring known ideal hardness results to the noisy setting without extra assumptions.
model_or_system: The model is Noisy Random Circuit Sampling (noisy RCS) applied to $n$-qubit circuits subjected to standard local depolarizing noise of strength $\gamma$. The analysis relies on comparing the noisy output probability to its ideal counterpart.
key_observables: Inverse-polynomial total variation distance (TVD) between the true and simulated sampling distributions, and the resulting hardness/simulability boundary scale.
important_parameters: Noise strength $\gamma$, number of qubits $n$, and circuit depth $d$. The critical asymptotic scale is identified as $\gamma = \Theta(\log n/(nd))$.
main_assumptions: The result assumes the standard average-case \#P-hardness conjecture for ideal RCS. It also relies on combining its hardness bound with existing simulability results for layered, regularly connected architectures.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a complexity phase diagram showing the established hard region (red) relative to known efficient simulation regimes under i.i.d. depolarizing noise.
paper_structure: The paper first defines the problem of noisy RCS hardness and then develops the mathematical machinery using polynomial extrapolation and monotonicity reduction. It applies these tools to transfer the ideal hardness conjecture to a specific, non-trivial noise strength $\gamma^*$. Finally, it combines this result with known simulability bounds to pinpoint the transition scale.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum advantage claims by quantifying how noise degrades computational hardness. For AMO/Open Quantum Systems researchers, understanding this boundary is crucial for designing fault-tolerant protocols or interpreting experimental results from noisy hardware.
